title: YAGNI and KISS
summary: Build only what today's one real case needs; delete the pluggable seam, the hooks and the config flag nobody uses.
signals: a `Strategy`/`Policy` interface with exactly one production implementation and no second caller
a factory or registry keyed by a config string that only ever has one entry registered
hook or callback lists (`onBefore*`, `onAfter*`) that are empty at every call site in the repo
a config flag that is read in exactly one place, or read nowhere at all, and never set to anything but its default

roles.OrderCancellationService: the abstraction built for a future that never arrived
roles.StandardCancellationPolicy: the only implementation that has ever existed
roles.CancellationPolicyRegistry: the pluggable seam nobody plugs a second thing into
roles.CancellationHooks: extension points nobody has wired up
roles.Order.canBeCancelled: what's left once the speculation is deleted

stages.title: Built for later
stages.idea: A registry, a hook list and a config flag exist for a policy that has exactly one implementation; a typo in the config key silently falls back instead of failing.

stages.title: Deleted to what's called
stages.idea: One method holds the one real rule; the same behavioural cases still pass, with far less to read.

checks: The registry only has one entry registered. What does keeping it cost a new hire who has to change the cancellation rule today?
A second cancellation policy shows up next sprint. Does that fact retroactively justify having built the interface early? What would justify building it now instead?
What is the 'rule of three' applied to abstractions rather than duplicated code, and what's the concrete second use case that would justify reintroducing a policy seam here?
YAGNI says 'don't build it yet' — explain why that is not the same advice as 'skip the tests' or 'skip refactoring'.
